q1.prompt: What is Snowflake's default Time Travel retention period on a Standard account?

a.feedback: Correct! The default is 1 day. Enterprise Edition and above can set up to 90 days per object with DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS.

b.feedback: Not quite — 90 days is the maximum on Enterprise Edition and above, not the default. The default is 1 day.

c.feedback: No — Time Travel only covers a retention window. Beyond it, history leaves Time Travel (and briefly enters Snowflake-managed Fail-safe).

d.feedback: No — retention is measured in days and survives your session. The default is 1 day.

q2.prompt: You ran a bad DELETE and captured its query id. Which clause shows the table exactly as it was immediately before that statement?

a.feedback: Correct! BEFORE(statement => ...) anchors to the state right before a specific statement — ideal when you know which query caused the damage.

b.feedback: There is no AFTER clause. Use BEFORE(statement => ...) to see the state just before a statement ran.

c.feedback: A positive offset points into the future, which isn't valid. Offsets are negative seconds (e.g. -60), and here BEFORE(statement=>) is the precise tool.

d.feedback: ROLLBACK only undoes an open transaction. Once a DELETE is committed, you recover with Time Travel (AT / BEFORE), not ROLLBACK.

q3.prompt: Why is CREATE TABLE ... CLONE ... BEFORE(statement => ...) the recommended way to recover an older state?

a.text: It makes a zero-copy clone of the good state you can inspect before swapping it in — without duplicating storage
a.feedback: Correct! Cloning is instant and zero-copy (storage is shared until data diverges), so you can verify the recovered table before touching the live one.

b.text: It permanently disables Time Travel on the table
b.feedback: No — cloning doesn't disable Time Travel. It creates a separate object you can inspect and then rename into place.

c.text: It physically copies every row, which is why it's slow but safe
c.feedback: The opposite — a clone is zero-copy and near-instant. Storage is only consumed as the clone and source diverge.

d.text: It emails your admin to restore a backup
d.feedback: No backups or admins are involved. Time Travel recovery is self-service and built in.

q4.prompt: You accidentally ran DROP TABLE ORDERS_ANALYSIS — the whole table, not just some rows. Still inside the retention window, what's the fastest way to get it back?

a.feedback: Correct! UNDROP restores a dropped table (or schema/database) in one line, as long as you're still within the retention window. AT/BEFORE and CLONE recover row-level changes; UNDROP recovers a dropped object.

b.text: Re-run CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT from the shared source
b.feedback: That rebuilds a table from the source, but it isn't Time Travel recovery — and it only matches if the source is unchanged. For a dropped object, UNDROP is the direct, exact restore.

c.text: Contact Snowflake Support to restore it from Fail-safe
c.feedback: Fail-safe is only for data past the retention window and is Support-only. A freshly dropped table is still in Time Travel — use UNDROP yourself.

d.text: Nothing — a dropped table is deleted immediately and permanently
d.feedback: No — a DROP is recoverable within the retention window. UNDROP TABLE brings it right back.

q1.prompt: A pipeline ran INSERT OVERWRITE on a staging table with a bad source, replacing all good rows. Within the retention window, how do you recover the prior state?

a.text: Query the table BEFORE(statement => '<overwrite_query_id>') and clone that state back
a.feedback: Correct! INSERT OVERWRITE replaces rows but the prior version stays in Time Travel. BEFORE(statement => ...) anchors to the state just before the overwrite, and you clone it back.

b.text: Nothing — INSERT OVERWRITE permanently discards the old rows
b.feedback: Not so — the pre-overwrite version is retained in Time Travel for the retention window and is fully recoverable.

c.text: Re-run the pipeline and hope the source is fixed
c.feedback: That doesn't restore what was lost if the source is still wrong. Time Travel recovers the exact prior state deterministically.

d.text: Open a Snowflake Support ticket to restore from Fail-safe
d.feedback: Fail-safe is a last resort after the Time Travel window closes. Within retention, you recover yourself with AT/BEFORE — no ticket.

q2.prompt: Why is a point-in-time CLONE well suited to building a backfill from a past state?

a.text: It's zero-copy and near-instant — you get a full copy of the historical state without duplicating storage
a.feedback: Correct! A clone shares storage with its source until they diverge, so cloning yesterday's state to re-derive a downstream table is cheap and fast.

b.text: It streams every row through the warehouse, which guarantees freshness
b.feedback: A clone doesn't copy rows — it's a metadata operation (zero-copy). That's exactly why it's fast and storage-light.

c.text: It permanently freezes the source table so it can't change
c.feedback: Cloning doesn't lock or freeze the source. It creates an independent object you can work with.

d.text: It automatically reruns all downstream tasks
d.feedback: A clone just materialises the historical state. Re-deriving downstream tables is a separate step you control.

q3.prompt: Your staging table's data retention is the default. How long do you have to self-recover a bad load with Time Travel before it leaves the window?

a.text: 1 day (default) — extendable up to 90 days on Enterprise+ via DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS
a.feedback: Correct! The default retention is 1 day. Raise DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS (up to 90 on Enterprise+) on tables whose loads you may need to recover further back.

b.feedback: No — Time Travel is bounded by the retention period. After it, data briefly enters Snowflake-managed Fail-safe, not self-service Time Travel.

c.feedback: Retention is measured in days and is independent of warehouse state. The default is 1 day.

d.feedback: The default is 1 day, not 7. You can raise it up to 90 on Enterprise+ per object.

q4.prompt: After a bad INSERT OVERWRITE clobbered ORDERS_STAGING, why clone the pre-overwrite state into a new table, verify it, and only then swap it in — instead of recovering straight over the live table?

a.text: Cloning to a separate table lets you verify the recovered rows before you touch the live table; the DROP + RENAME swap then puts good data back under the same name downstream jobs already read
a.feedback: Correct! Verify-then-swap means you never overwrite the live object until you're sure, and renaming the good clone into place keeps the object name downstream depends on.

b.text: It's required syntax — you can't apply BEFORE(...) directly to the live table
b.feedback: Not true — you can query the live table with BEFORE(...). The clone-verify-swap pattern is about safety and keeping the object name stable, not a syntax limit.

c.text: Cloning permanently locks ORDERS_STAGING so no other job can overwrite it again
c.feedback: A clone doesn't lock or freeze the source. The live table stays writable; the pattern just protects you until you've verified the recovery.

d.text: Recovering in place is impossible — Time Travel can only write to brand-new tables
d.feedback: Time Travel can recover into the same table too. The point of clone-verify-swap is to confirm the good state before replacing live data.

q1.prompt: A cleanup script accidentally ran DROP SCHEMA on a live schema minutes ago. What's the fastest recovery within the retention window?

a.text: UNDROP SCHEMA — it instantly restores the schema and all objects inside it
a.feedback: Correct! UNDROP works at table, schema, and database scope. UNDROP SCHEMA brings the whole schema back with its contents — no rebuild needed.

b.text: Recreate the schema and reload every table by hand
b.feedback: Slow and error-prone. Within retention, UNDROP SCHEMA restores everything in one statement.

c.feedback: Snowflake doesn't rely on nightly backups for this. UNDROP recovers the dropped schema directly.

d.text: Nothing — dropping a schema is irreversible
d.feedback: Not within the retention window. UNDROP SCHEMA reverses an accidental drop.

a.text: The Time Travel retention window for an object (or account) — how far back you can AT/BEFORE/UNDROP
a.feedback: Correct! It sets the retention window. Default is 1 day; Enterprise+ allows up to 90 days, set at account, database, schema, or table level.

b.text: How long query results stay in the result cache
b.feedback: That's a separate mechanism. DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS governs Time Travel retention, not result caching.

c.text: How long before a warehouse auto-suspends
c.feedback: Auto-suspend is a warehouse setting (AUTO_SUSPEND). DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS governs Time Travel.

d.text: How long Fail-safe keeps data after Time Travel ends
d.feedback: Fail-safe is a fixed, Snowflake-managed period and is not configurable. This parameter controls the self-service Time Travel window.

q3.prompt: How do Time Travel and Fail-safe differ for an admin planning recovery?

a.text: Time Travel is self-service within the retention window; Fail-safe is a short, non-configurable period recoverable only by Snowflake Support
a.feedback: Correct! Design recovery around Time Travel (you control it). Fail-safe is a last-resort safety net you can't query or configure.

b.text: They're the same feature with two names
b.feedback: No — Time Travel is self-service and configurable; Fail-safe is Snowflake-managed and not self-service.

c.text: Fail-safe is longer and fully self-service
c.feedback: Fail-safe is not self-service — only Snowflake Support can recover from it, and it's a fixed short window.

d.text: Time Travel only works on tables; Fail-safe only on schemas
d.feedback: Both operate at object level. The real difference is self-service (Time Travel) vs Snowflake-managed last resort (Fail-safe).

q4.prompt: You set DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 7 on a database, but a table inside it has it set to 1. What retention applies to that table?

a.text: 1 day — the parameter resolves at account/database/schema/table level, and the most specific level (the table) wins
a.feedback: Correct! DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS is inherited down the hierarchy, but the most specific setting overrides. The table's own value of 1 wins over the database's 7.

b.text: 7 days — a database-level setting always overrides its tables
b.feedback: Backwards — inheritance flows down, but the most specific level wins. The table's own value overrides the database default.

c.feedback: Retention settings don't accumulate. Exactly one value is in effect: the most specific one, here the table's 1 day.

d.text: The account default — object-level settings are ignored
d.feedback: Object-level settings are honored and take precedence over broader defaults. The table's explicit 1 day is what applies.
